site.reason: split() with no argument treats any run of whitespace as one separator and drops leading and trailing empties; Java split(" ") splits on every single space and keeps a leading empty string.

flags.assumption: Using Scanner.nextInt() assumes the input consists of whitespace-separated integers matching Python's split() behavior, and further assumes at least n integers follow n and all values fit in 32-bit int.
flags.reasoning: Python uses open(0).read().split() to split on arbitrary runs of whitespace and ignore leading/trailing whitespace. Java uses Scanner.nextInt() in lines 6-11, which skips arbitrary whitespace delimiters in the same way.

site.reason: Python // rounds down (-7 // 2 is -4); Java integer / rounds toward zero (-7 / 2 is -3). Math.floorDiv matches Python.

flags.assumption: Using ans / 3 assumes ans is non-negative so truncating division matches floor division; this holds because tmp is never negative, provided n is small enough that ans does not overflow 32-bit int.
flags.reasoning: Python's // rounds toward negative infinity while Java's / truncates toward zero, which only differs for negative dividends. In the loop, tmp starts at max(0, right - left) and subtracts 1 only for distinct indices i and j inside [left, right), so tmp >= 0 and ans >= 0 unless ans overflows int.
